stimulus.text:
J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer, Letter III, “What Is an American?”, 1782:

“What then is the American, this new man? He is either an European, or the descendant of an European, hence that strange mixture of blood, which you will find in no other country. I could point out to you a family whose grandfather was an Englishman, whose wife was Dutch, whose son married a French woman, and whose present four sons have now four wives of different nations. He is an American, who leaving behind him all his ancient prejudices and manners, receives new ones from the new mode of life he has embraced, the new government he obeys, and the new rank he holds. ... Here individuals of all nations are melted into a new race of men, whose labours and posterity will one day cause great changes in the world. ... The American is a new man, who acts upon new principles; he must therefore entertain new ideas, and form new opinions.”
stimulus.source_note: J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer (1782), Letter III. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus quoted verbatim from J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer (1782), Letter III. Public domain.

primary_sources: J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer (1782), Letter III

stem: Crèvecœur’s description best supports which conclusion about American identity in the 1780s?

options.text: American identity rested mainly on loyalty to a king.
options.misconception: Background: the United States had broken with the king in 1776, and Crèvecœur describes a people living under a new government.

options.text: American identity was fixed at birth by a person’s European nationality.
options.misconception: The passage says the American receives new manners from his new mode of life.

options.text: American identity came mainly from the wealth of the colonies’ great cities.
options.misconception: The passage stresses principles and the new mode of life, not city wealth.

options.text: American identity was being built from shared life under a new government.

rationales.D: The passage shows many nations melting into one people who act on new principles under a new government.
rationales.A: The passage describes a people under a new government, not loyal subjects of a king.
rationales.B: Crèvecœur says the American leaves old manners behind and takes up new ones.
rationales.C: The passage says nothing about cities or wealth as the source of identity.
rationales.general:
1. The passage says people of all nations are melted into a new race of men.
2. It says the American acts upon new principles and forms new opinions.
3. Background: the passage was written in 1782, after independence but before the Constitution was written.
4. So identity here is made by shared life under a new government, not inherited from one European nation.
Remember: a national identity can be built from shared experience, not only from shared ancestry.
